items.title: TimedOutboxSweeper misses ticks when pool threads are blocked, and one Task.Run per publish confirm delays MarkDispatched under load
items.body:
### Describe the bug

Some teams use `Post`/`PostAsync` with the `InMemoryOutbox` and a producer whose publisher confirms arrive out of band, most often Kafka. In that setup the message is only marked dispatched when the confirm arrives, and anything never confirmed has to be re-sent by `TimedOutboxSweeper` running in the same process. We have reports that under load on Kubernetes (EKS) the sweeper runs rarely or not at all, so unconfirmed messages pile up in memory and are lost if the pod restarts.

We couldn't reproduce it on demand, so we measured each candidate cause separately. Every experiment uses the real `TimedOutboxSweeper` with `TimerInterval = 1` on net9.0 with `DOTNET_PROCESSOR_COUNT` constrained.

**1. The sweeper's tick runs on the shared thread pool and is late whenever pool threads are blocked.**

`TimedOutboxSweeper.StartAsync` creates a `System.Threading.Timer` whose callback is `async void Sweep` (`TimedOutboxSweeper.cs:77`, `:104`). The callback runs on a pool thread; the comment at `:128` ("on a timer thread, so blocking is OK") is wrong. With 200 pool work items blocked:

| Tick source | procs = 1 | procs = 2 |
|---|---|---|
| `TimedOutboxSweeper` (pool `Timer`) | 7 ticks in 10 s, max gap 3.03 s | 6 ticks, max gap 3.01 s |
| `PeriodicTimer` async loop | 4 ticks, max gap 2.00 s | 5 ticks, max gap 3.02 s |
| Dedicated thread | 10 ticks, max gap 1.00 s | 10 ticks, max gap 1.02 s |

So a plain `BackgroundService` awaiting a `PeriodicTimer` would not fix this. Only a dedicated thread kept time.

A long queue alone did not delay the tick. With 100k+ short `Task.Run` items pending, the sweeper still ticked every 1.00 s; the runtime appears to queue timer firings ahead of ordinary pool work. The tick only slips when workers are busy or blocked.

**2. `KafkaMessageProducer` (and `RmqMessageProducer` in RMQ.Sync) queue one `Task.Run` per delivery report.**

See `KafkaMessageProducer.RaisePublishConfirmation` (`:456`) and `RMQ.Sync/RmqMessageProducer.cs:282-307`. This doesn't starve the tick under normal load. Under overload, though, pending work grew by about one item per `Post`, `MarkDispatched` fell behind, and the sweeper re-sent messages that had in fact been delivered: about 100 re-sends per sweep in our run. Confirms should be drained through a bounded channel by one long-running worker (as `InMemoryMessageProducer` already does) rather than one pool item each.

**3. The sweeper has no protection against failure.**
- An exception rethrown from `OutboxProducerMediator.BackgroundDispatchUsingAsync` (`:762`), for example a `ConfigurationException` from producer lookup, escapes `async void Sweep` and crashes the process, taking the in-memory outbox with it. `TimedOutboxArchiver` catches everything (`:129-132`); the sweeper doesn't.
- `CreateScope()` (`TimedOutboxSweeper.cs:111`) is outside the `try`. If it throws, for example during shutdown, the `InMemoryLock` is never released, and every later tick logs "Outbox Sweeper is still running - abandoning attempt" for good.
- `TimerInterval` isn't validated. 0 sweeps once and never again; a negative value makes `StartAsync` throw.
- No cancellation token or timeout reaches the sweep (`OutboxSweeper.cs:79`, `TimedOutboxSweeper.cs:124`). A degraded broker can hold one 100-message sweep for minutes (5 s `MessageTimeoutMs` per message).

**4. You can't see any of this in telemetry.**

Nothing records tick lag (when the tick was due vs. when `Sweep` ran), sweep duration, messages found per sweep, or the abandon/skip events (`TimedOutboxSweeper.cs:136`, `OutboxProducerMediator.cs:775`, which are logs only). Draft PR #4484 adds outbox added/cleared counts and publish duration, which is complementary; this issue covers the sweeper's own health signals.

### Related

- **#4554:** the outstanding-message check runs on every `Post` under DI defaults. We hit the same defect; that issue covers it, and this one doesn't duplicate it. It is one source of the pool blocking in (1): each check parks a pool thread in a synchronous `.Wait()` on a static semaphore (`OutboxProducerMediator.cs:1334`). Details are in a comment there.
- **#4552:** adds `GetAwaiter().GetResult()` inside the same check for async-only outboxes.
- **#4484:** outbox metrics (draft).

### Proposed scope

- **Run the sweeper on a dedicated thread.**
  - Add an optional `TimeProvider` parameter; source compatibility only.
  - Make `Sweep` public and awaitable so it can be tested.
  - Catch everything inside the sweep.
  - Release the lock on every path.
  - Validate `TimerInterval`.
  - Pass a cancellation token to the sweep.
- **Drain Kafka and RMQ.Sync confirms through a bounded channel** instead of one `Task.Run` per delivery report.
- **Add OpenTelemetry metrics for the sweeper:** tick lag, sweep duration, messages found, abandon/skip counts.
- **Add a harness under `samples/`** that reproduces Post + InMemoryOutbox + async confirms under constrained CPU and shows the new telemetry.

### To Reproduce

Two scratch console apps, which we'll turn into the `samples/` harness:
- **Tick latency:** start a `TimedOutboxSweeper` whose `IDistributedLock` records each `ObtainLockAsync` call, park 200 `Task.Run(() => gate.Wait())` items, and compare its ticks with a dedicated-thread loop. Run with `DOTNET_PROCESSOR_COUNT=1` or `2`.
- **Full pipeline:** `CommandProcessor` + `OutboxProducerMediator` + `InMemoryOutbox` + `TimedOutboxSweeper`, with a fake producer that delivers on a non-pool thread and calls `Task.Run` per confirm, as Kafka does. Use 64 concurrent posters.

### Further technical details

- Brighter: master at `2890f8610`, V10.X
- Observed: EKS under CPU limits. Measured: macOS, .NET 9, `DOTNET_PROCESSOR_COUNT` = 1 / 2

---
Analysis and experiments were prepared with the help of an AI assistant.

items.title: Improve Getting Started and Building Apps for enterprise architecture evaluation
items.body:
> *This was generated by AI during triage.*

## Tell us about your request

Improve the Getting Started and Building Apps documentation for experienced Java developers and architects evaluating Vaadin for an enterprise project.

The current documentation provides enough guidance to build a convincing prototype, but leaves important architectural and operational questions unanswered along the main learning path. It demonstrates developer productivity more convincingly than it explains the commitment involved in adopting and operating Vaadin.

This review is based on `main` at `f42ae9b6a`. It is a documentation assessment, not a runtime benchmark. Some gaps below are missing guidance; others are discoverability problems where relevant material already exists elsewhere.

### Preserve what already works

- The quick start demonstrates components, event listeners, use of a Java library, and a production JAR.
- Building Apps contains substantial guidance on application services, DTOs versus entities, transactions, optimistic locking, database migrations, and paginated grids.
- Background jobs and server push address real concerns such as threading, cleanup, memory leaks, and excessive updates.
- Browserless testing guides cover several application frameworks and realistic interactions.

## Findings, in priority order

### 1. Introduce the runtime model and its architectural consequences early

An evaluator needs to understand where UI state lives, what happens on a button click, what is stored per user and per tab, which interactions require server round trips, and what happens when connectivity or a session is lost.

The [quick start](https://github.com/vaadin/docs/blob/f42ae9b6aa3cf6873707fdbd0fa4e564e039000f/articles/getting-started/quick-start/index.adoc#L255) explains that Java UI code runs on the server, and [Conceptual Layers](https://github.com/vaadin/docs/blob/f42ae9b6aa3cf6873707fdbd0fa4e564e039000f/articles/building-apps/architecture/layers.adoc#L17) explains the UI/application distinction. Neither provides a compact operational model covering state, latency, concurrency, and deployment.

**Suggested improvement:** Add a prominently linked “How a Vaadin application works” explanation with a request-flow diagram, session/UI lifetimes, and practical implications. Include guidance on suitability and the situations where client-side React views are useful.

### 2. Surface stateful deployment and scaling tradeoffs in Architecture

The architecture section discusses monoliths, microservices, and packaging, but the Vaadin-specific consequences of scaling are more important to an adoption decision than general architectural definitions.

The [distributed deployment reference](https://github.com/vaadin/docs/blob/f42ae9b6aa3cf6873707fdbd0fa4e564e039000f/articles/flow/production/distributed-deployment.adoc#L36) already explains sticky sessions, replication, serialization constraints, and Kubernetes Kit. Architecture should lead readers to it before they make deployment assumptions.

**Suggested improvement:** Explain how to evaluate:
- Memory consumption per active session and realistic concurrent-user workloads.
- Interaction latency under realistic network conditions.
- User experience during node failure, scale-down, and deployment.
- Session continuity, session draining, and accepting a reload as operational choices.

Provide a practical measurement approach rather than a universal concurrency claim.

### 3. Complete the route from tutorial to production

Creating a production JAR is covered. Operating an application is not presented as a coherent next step.

[Next Steps](https://github.com/vaadin/docs/blob/f42ae9b6aa3cf6873707fdbd0fa4e564e039000f/articles/getting-started/next-steps.adoc#L9) links to views, data, security, a real database, and agentic development, but lacks an explicit route through testing, deployment, monitoring, and failure handling. Production documentation exists under Flow Reference.

**Suggested improvement:** Add a “Take this application to production” path covering production builds, containers, reverse proxies and push connections, environment configuration and secrets, health checks, logs and metrics, and CI. Reuse and link existing reference material.

### 4. Connect security guidance to enterprise authentication and authorization

[Add Login](https://github.com/vaadin/docs/blob/f42ae9b6aa3cf6873707fdbd0fa4e564e039000f/articles/building-apps/security/add-login.adoc#L12) teaches in-memory authentication and refers production readers to Spring Security documentation. Connecting an enterprise identity provider is likely an early proof-of-concept task.

A concrete [OAuth2/Keycloak guide](https://github.com/vaadin/docs/blob/f42ae9b6aa3cf6873707fdbd0fa4e564e039000f/articles/flow/integrations/spring/oauth2.adoc#L10) already exists, including role mapping, but Add Login does not link to it.

**Suggested improvement:** Provide a clear route from login setup to an enterprise identity provider, role mapping, logout, and security verification. Extend the guidance beyond roles with an example of record-level authorization (“this user may edit this customer”) and guidance or explicit scope boundaries for tenant isolation.

[Protect Services](https://github.com/vaadin/docs/blob/f42ae9b6aa3cf6873707fdbd0fa4e564e039000f/articles/building-apps/security/protect-services.adoc#L51) also instructs readers to test method security while saying that the corresponding guide is not yet written. Complete that handoff.

### 5. Offer a faster evaluation route and a clear tutorial conclusion

The tutorial includes useful explanations, complete code per step, and realistic concerns such as optimistic locking. However, it asks for [20–45 minutes per step](https://github.com/vaadin/docs/blob/f42ae9b6aa3cf6873707fdbd0fa4e564e039000f/articles/getting-started/tutorial/index.adoc#L16), and the reviewed tutorial pages do not link to a runnable finished tutorial repository.

The tutorial [ends with a promise of more steps](https://github.com/vaadin/docs/blob/f42ae9b6aa3cf6873707fdbd0fa4e564e039000f/articles/getting-started/tutorial/deep-link.adoc#L1312), while [Building Apps opens with a work-in-progress notice](https://github.com/vaadin/docs/blob/f42ae9b6aa3cf6873707fdbd0fa4e564e039000f/articles/building-apps/index.adoc#L13). Together these weaken confidence in the completeness of the recommended development path.

**Suggested improvement:** Give the tutorial a clearly bounded outcome and useful conclusion. Provide a runnable reference application with authentication, a service boundary, a database migration, representative tests, and deployment instructions so experienced readers can inspect it before following the tutorial selectively.

### 6. Make commercial boundaries and maintenance considerations discoverable

An evaluator needs to distinguish capabilities available in the open-source core from commercial components, tools, operational kits, and support offerings.

Relevant information exists elsewhere: the [testing reference](https://github.com/vaadin/docs/blob/f42ae9b6aa3cf6873707fdbd0fa4e564e039000f/articles/flow/testing/index.adoc#L13) explains that browserless testing is free and discusses TestBench, Selenium, and Playwright; [Kubernetes Kit](https://github.com/vaadin/docs/blob/f42ae9b6aa3cf6873707fdbd0fa4e564e039000f/articles/tools/kubernetes/index.adoc#L11) is marked commercial.

**Suggested improvement:** Provide an evaluation-oriented capability map and links to supported technologies, release support, upgrades, and licensing. Make technical and procurement dependencies understandable without duplicating pricing information throughout the tutorials.

### 7. Distinguish framework requirements from recommended defaults

[Project Structure](https://github.com/vaadin/docs/blob/f42ae9b6aa3cf6873707fdbd0fa4e564e039000f/articles/building-apps/architecture/project-structure/index.adoc#L12) describes a Vaadin project as essentially Spring Boot and Maven, while other documentation supports plain Java, CDI, Quarkus, and Gradle. The recommended stack is reasonable, but should be explicitly identified as a recommendation.

The [microservices guide](https://github.com/vaadin/docs/blob/f42ae9b6aa3cf6873707fdbd0fa4e564e039000f/articles/building-apps/architecture/microservices.adoc#L52) says a separate API gateway is unnecessary because Vaadin can call services directly. Direct calls alone do not settle gateway requirements for routing, policy, or traffic management.

**Suggested improvement:** Review architectural wording to distinguish Vaadin constraints, recommended defaults, and choices that depend on the surrounding system.

## Additional gaps to address or explicitly signpost

- Consuming existing remote services, including timeouts and failure handling. The current [Integration guide](https://github.com/vaadin/docs/blob/f42ae9b6aa3cf6873707fdbd0fa4e564e039000f/articles/building-apps/integration/rest-api.adoc#L10) focuses on exposing an API.
- Application-wide error handling and recovery.
- Accessibility verification and internationalization.
- A testing strategy combining service, database, browserless, and browser tests.

## Proposed outcome

Create an architect’s evaluation path, reachable from Getting Started and Building Apps, that connects runtime architecture and suitability, state and scaling, enterprise identity, testing and deployment, and commercial/support boundaries.

Use this issue to coordinate the documentation improvements; the individual topics can be implemented separately.

### Acceptance criteria

- [ ] An experienced Java developer can find the evaluation path from both entry points without knowing the reference documentation structure.
- [ ] The path explains Vaadin’s runtime model and the consequences of stateful UIs before deployment decisions are made.
- [ ] Existing deployment, OAuth2, testing, compatibility, and licensing material is linked at the relevant decision points.
- [ ] The tutorial has a clear conclusion and a route to a secured, tested, deployed application.
- [ ] A runnable reference application is linked for readers who want to inspect a complete example first.
- [ ] Architectural recommendations are clearly distinguished from framework requirements.
- [ ] Remaining gaps are explicitly identified, with concrete next steps rather than broad promises of future content.

---

If you think this issue is important, add a 👍 [reaction](https://blog.github.com/2016-03-10-add-reactions-to-pull-requests-issues-and-comments/) to help the community and maintainers prioritize this issue.
